newsitem.title: UK: Two-year Protestant N.Irish truce hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: Two-year Protestant N.Irish truce hangs in balance.

text.p: A truce by pro-British protestant "Loyalists" hung in the balance on Saturday, the eve of its second anniversary, after a British soldier died from injuries from an IRA bombing.

Protestant sources said the guerrillas' umbrella group, the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), met on Friday to decide its future stance. No statement was issued but the sources said one might be released over the weekend.

Fears that Loyalists might abandon their truce grew when their arch foes, the Irish Republican Army (IRA), struck at the heart of Britain's military presence last Monday with two car bombs at army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast.
Some 30 troops and civilians were wounded. A loyalist source told Reuters that the death on Friday of one of the wounded soldiers might "tip the balance" towards renewed conflict.
"I think it's in the air at the moment. It was at the wire, I don't know whether they have stepped over," Eddie Kinner, a Loyalist political activist told BBC television.
Others were cautiously optimistic the guerrilla commanders would resist a return to the random killings of Catholic nationalists or planting bombs in neighbouring Catholic Ireland.

Alarmed at the prospect of a slide into sectarian warfare, political leaders in Britain, Ireland and the U.S. have implored Loyalists to maintain their stance of non-violence which has won their political spokesman seats in peace talks.

The guerrillas' legal political wings have added their voices to the peace appeals, saying Loyalists must not fall into a trap set by an IRA intent on turning the clock back to all-out conflict. The IRA denies trying to provoke them.
The IRA attack was its first in Northern Ireland since it declared a truce in September 1994.
The Loyalist ceasefire declared six weeks later on October 13, 1994, seemed to signal an end to years of strife that had claimed more than 3,200 lives.
But optimism soured quickly as the government and Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, wrangled over Britain's demands for all guerrilla groups to surrender weapons before full talks.
The IRA accused Britain of reneging on a guarantee of a place in talks and set off a bomb in London in February 1996, ending its truce.
Britain and Ireland launched multi-party talks on a new settlement in June but said that while the IRA was wedded to war, Sinn Fein would not be given a seat.
Loyalist politicians say that if Protestant guerrillas break their truce, Britain and Ireland might retaliate by expelling them from the talks, currently making slow progress in Belfast.
The Loyalist groups threaten to safeguard British rule by terrorising Catholics into pressing the IRA to call off its campaign for a united Irish state ruled from Dublin.
Hopes for continued peace rest with the emergence of a new "political Loyalism" in the two-year truce lull.
Analysts say the guerrillas' political wings have espoused their case for a "British Northern Ireland" with a fluency and moderation that has won them respect they previously lacked.
